name: Short Almost Perfect Scale
domain: Self talk, thinking patterns and personality
construct: Perfectionistic high personal standards and the perceived discrepancy between performance and those standards.
licence: Rice lab statement: no permission is required to use or translate the SAPS because it is a subset of the APS-R; cite properly. The PDF carries no copyright notice, only the citation.
instructions: The following items are designed to measure certain attitudes people have toward themselves, their performance, and toward others. It is important that your answers be true and accurate for you. In the space next to the statement, please enter a number from "1" (strongly disagree) to "7" (strongly agree) to describe your degree of agreement with each item.

items.text: I have high expectations for myself.
Doing my best never seems to be enough.
I set very high standards for myself.
I often feel disappointment after completing a task because I know I could have done better.
I have a strong need to strive for excellence.
My performance rarely measures up to my standards.
I expect the best from myself.
I am hardly ever satisfied with my performance.

subscales.name: Discrepancy
subscales.description: Perceived gap between performance and standards; the maladaptive component of perfectionism.

scoring: Sum (4 to 28) or average (1 to 7) the items within each subscale as printed in the source key: "Standards = 1, 3, 5, 7" and "Discrepancy = 2, 4, 6, 8". No items are reverse scored. Higher Discrepancy indicates more maladaptive perfectionism; higher Standards indicates higher personal standards. No SAPS specific cut offs are published.
citation: Rice, K. G., Richardson, C. M. E., & Tueller, S. (2014). The Short Form of the Revised Almost Perfect Scale. Journal of Personality Assessment, 96(3), 368–379. https://doi.org/10.1080/00223891.2013.838172
transcriptionNote: Transcribed from the SAPS-English.pdf hosted by Kenneth Wang, titled "SAPS (Short Almost Perfect Scale)". All 8 items, the instructions, the 7 anchor labels (printed in capitals) and the scoring key were read in full. No uncertainties.
